Series::cummax¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::cummax() const -> Series
Series::cummax(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

cummax() computes a running maximum along one axis.

Like cumsum() it is a scan, not a reduction: the axis keeps its full length, and each position is replaced by the largest value seen from the start of the axis up to and including that position.

For a row [1, 3, 2, 5, 4] the running maximum is [1, 3, 3, 5, 5] — it never decreases, and it “latches” onto each new record until a larger one appears.

The no-argument form scans axis 0. Pass dim to scan a different axis; negative values count from the back.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t, optional)

The axis to scan. Omitted: axis 0. Negative values count from the back. The result keeps the same shape, because a scan does not remove an axis.

Returns¶

Series The running maximum along dim, with the same shape and dtype as the input (an integer series stays integer).

Gradient¶

cummax() is differentiable.

Its backward routes the sensitivity of each output position to the single input position that held the running maximum there. Formally, d/dx_i cummax(x)[t] is 1 when i is the position of the running max at t and 0 otherwise, so a value that stays the record for a long stretch collects the gradient of every output in that stretch. On a tie the earliest position keeps the record, matching the forward.

Examples¶

The examples build up from the basic scan to the axis argument and the backward.

Example 1. The running maximum of a 1-D row.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 5.0, 4.0}).cummax(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 3.0000, 3.0000, 5.0000, 5.0000]

The 2 and the 4 never appear in the output — the running maximum has already passed them.

Example 2. dim selects the axis; each lane is scanned independently.

auto m = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 4.0, 2.0},
    {3.0, 2.0, 5.0},
});

std::cout << "dim 0:\n" << m.cummax(0);
std::cout << "\ndim 1:\n" << m.cummax(1);

Output¶

dim 0:
pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 4, 2],
  [3, 4, 5]]
dim 1:
pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 4, 4],
  [3, 3, 5]]

Down the columns the running max compares row 0 with row 1. Across the rows it walks left to right.

Example 3. Integer input keeps its dtype.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1, 3, 2, 5}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64).cummax(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 3, 3, 5]

Example 4. A NaN never becomes the running maximum, so the scan carries the last real record past it.

double nan = std::nan("");

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, nan, 3.0, 2.0}).cummax(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000, 3.0000]

Example 5. The backward sends each output’s sensitivity to the position that held the record.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 5.0, 4.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.cummax(0).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

dx=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 0, 2, 0]

Position 1 held the record at outputs 1 and 2, so it collects 2. Position 3 held it at outputs 3 and 4, so it also collects 2. Positions 2 and 4 were never the record and get 0.

Example 6. On a tie the earliest position keeps the record and so keeps the gradient.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, 3.0, 2.0, 4.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.cummax(0).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

dx=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[3, 0, 0, 1]

The second 3 never strictly exceeds the first, so position 0 stays the record through outputs 0, 1, and 2.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • cummax() is a scan: the output keeps the full axis length. To collapse the axis to a single maximum, use max().

  • A NaN is skipped by the running comparison rather than propagated. If you need NaN-aware behavior, screen the input first.

  • Ties keep the earliest position, both in the forward output and in the gradient.

Summary¶

cummax(x) is the running maximum along an axis:

  • shape- and dtype-preserving scan; default axis is 0

  • monotonically non-decreasing along the scanned axis

  • differentiable: each output’s sensitivity flows to the position that held the record, ties to the earliest

See Also¶

  • Series::cummin: the running minimum.

  • Series::max: the whole-axis maximum, which removes the axis.

  • Series::cumsum: the additive prefix scan.
